title: Early paid gigs and the family band repertoire
summary: They earned about five dollars a wedding in 1954-55; the book was swing, stock arrangements, Italian tunes and transcribed solos.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: So you were playing gigs at an early age. Did they pay you?

We used to get five dollars sometimes, which was pretty good in 1954, ’55 you know. But the jobs were like you played 55 minutes on and 5 minutes off, basically, for weddings. So I mean you were just going, going, going all the time. Yeah. I mean I © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
started working in ’54 I think, ’54 yeah. I was eight. I was eight years old. And my brother Joe was probably working when he was around six or seven, maybe six.
What was the set list like at that time? You probably were playing Swing Era tunes but also maybe whatever was on the radio?

Swing and pop music of the day, Glenn Miller stocks, a lot of them were stock arrangements, a lot of Italian tunes. If it was Italian weddings we had to play all of the traditional Italian mazurkas and polkas. And so he had a whole library of that Italian music. And then the pop music of the day you know, which was in the 50s, and a lot of the stuff was — you had some funny stuff — but a lot of it was swing. He had quite a few stocks from the 30s and 40s basically, because he had his own dance band at one time so he had ordered all the stock arrangements. So you know we had “In the Mood” and “String of Pearls” and The Casa Loma Orchestra stuff, and you know he had bunches of books of jazz transcriptions, Frankie Trumbauer solo books, and Chu Berry solo books, and Toots Mondello books you know, so we had all of these transcribed solos that he would give us to read.
